cards.explanation: The answer is Ahab's silver and gold and his family. Ben-hadad, king of Aram, sends word to Ahab, king of Israel: “Your silver and gold are mine, and your best wives and children are mine!” (1 Kings 20:3) Silver, gold, family. That's the whole list, friends, and Ben-hadad doesn't ask nicely, either.

The answer is that Ahab agrees to all of it. Ahab, king of Israel, says, “Just as you say, my lord the king: I am yours, along with all that I have.” That's a yes to everything on the list. I think saying that out loud with an army outside had to be a rough moment. Keep it in mind, because Ahab's answer changes when the second message comes.

The answer is False. Ben-hadad says, “But about this time tomorrow I will send my servants to search your palace…” That's one day, not a week. His servants will search the palace and the houses of Ahab's servants, and they'll carry away what is precious to Ahab.

The answer is elders. Ahab summons “…all the elders of the land…” He tells them Ben-hadad is looking for trouble, because when Ben-hadad demanded his wives, children, silver and gold, Ahab did not deny him. Smart move, friends, calling in the whole table before answering.

The answer is don't listen and don't agree. The elders and the people all say, “Do not listen to him or consent to his terms.” That's a clear answer from everybody at the table. Ahab had already said yes to the first demand, and now the elders and the people tell him to refuse these terms. I think it's a crowd that has had enough.

The answer is False. Ahab doesn't take anything back. He says, “All that you demanded of your servant the first time I will do, but this thing I cannot do.” His yes to the first demand stands, friends. The no is only for the second demand.

The answer is that Samaria will be crushed to dust. Ben-hadad swears, “May the gods deal with me, and ever so severely, if enough dust remains of Samaria for each of my men to have a handful.” That's his threat: not enough dust left of Samaria for each of his men to take a handful. That's a lot of threat packed into one sentence. Remember that he's the one doing the swearing.

The answer is drinking. The text says Ben-hadad got Ahab's message “…while he and the kings were drinking in their tents…” That's thirty-three kings, counting Ben-hadad, in tents with cups. I think it's worth noticing where they are when that message reaches them. Hold that picture, friends, because it comes back later in the story.

The answer is True. Ben-hadad hears Ahab's message and tells his servants, “Take your positions.” So they station themselves against the city. No long speech, no second oath. Just orders, and his servants take their places.

The answer is that the LORD will deliver the army into Ahab's hand this very day. A prophet comes to Ahab with a word from the LORD: “Behold, I will deliver it into your hand this very day, and you will know that I am the LORD.” This very day, friends. The army that looked like the end of Samaria is the one the LORD says He'll hand over.

The answer is the young officers of the district governors. Ahab asks, “By whom?” and the prophet answers, “This is what the LORD says: ‘By the young officers of the district governors.’…” So the LORD names the young officers who serve under the governors of the districts. Not the whole army, not the top brass. I think Ahab had to take a breath at that answer.

The answer is Ahab. Ahab asks, “Who will start the battle?” and the prophet answers, “You will.” So the king himself starts it. He's the one who said yes to everything on Ben-hadad's first list. Now the one who gave in is the one who starts the fight.

The answer is False. The 232 are in front, but they have company. Ahab assembles “…the rest of the Israelite troops, 7,000 in all.” The text says the army is behind the young officers as they march out of the city. It's a small crew up front, with a bigger one at their backs.

The answer is True, friends. The text says Israel marched out at noon “…while Ben-hadad and the 32 kings allied with him were in their tents getting drunk.” Thirty-three kings, in the tents, at noon. That's the picture the text gives us.

The answer is to take them alive either way. Ben-hadad says, “If they have marched out in peace,” and then, “take them alive. Even if they have marched out for war, take them alive.” Peace or war, the order is the same. I think that's a king who is sure of himself. Hold that thought, friends, and watch how things go.

The answer is flee. Each of the young officers strikes down his opponent, “So the Arameans fled, with the Israelites in pursuit.” The word is fled. The Arameans were the ones with the big army and the oath about dust. Now they're the ones running.

The answer is False, friends. Nobody takes Ben-hadad captive. As the Arameans flee, Ben-hadad king of Aram “…escaped on horseback with the cavalry.” He's the one who had told his men to take others alive. Now he's the one riding away, and the story isn't done with him yet.
